newsitem.title: USA: Senate pushes ahead with Clinton cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Senate pushes ahead with Clinton cabinet.

text.p: The Senate, with little dissent and much praise, continued Wednesday to act swiftly to put President Clinton's second-term Cabinet in place.

By a vote of 99-0, it confirmed Andrew Cuomo to be secretary of housing and urban development. By exactly the same margins last week it approved Madeleine Albright as secretary of state and William Cohen as defence secretary.
Meanwhile, the Senate Commerce Committee voted 15-1 to support William Daley nomination as commerce secretary, sending it to the full Senate for a vote Thursday morning.
Three other nominees testified to Senate committees and appeared headed for easy approval.

Representative Bill Richardson, a Democratic from New Mexico, known for his humanitarian missions to negotiate with authoritarian regimes from Sudan to Burma to North Korea, found himself among friends as he testified to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on his nomination as United Nations ambassador.
Although his formal printed statement to the committee called him "William," Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, told him, "I'm going to call you 'Bill.'"
"It's a great start when the chairman calls you 'Bill,'" Democrat Joseph Biden of Delaware said.
In the Senate Finance Committee the nominee for U.S. trade representative, Charlene Barshefsky, had strong bipartisan support, according to the chairman, Republican William Roth of Delaware.
After a friendly hearing Wednesday, the committee is to vote Thursday on Barshefsky's nomination and will also consider legislation exempting her from a law that would prevent her taking office.
The law bars anyone from the trade post who has represented a foreign government on trade matters. As a Washington lawyer, Barshefsky represented Canadian lumber interests.

Federal Highway Administrator Rodney Slater sailed easily through a Senate Commerce Committee hearing on his nomination to be transportation secretary after getting high marks from senators of both parties.

The Energy Committee is to hold a nomination hearing Thursday for former Transportation Secretary Federico Pena to be energy secretary and the Senate Banking Committee is to hold a hearing Feb. 5 on the nomination of Federal Reserve Governor Janet Yellen to head the Council of Economic Advisers.

The Senate Labour Committee has not yet set a hearing on the nomination of Alexis Herman to be labour secretary. Republicans have criticised her connection to a Democratic Party fundraising controversy.
But White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Wednesday Clinton was willing to work hard for a nominee he considered to be exceptionally well qualified.
The most controversial nomination to go to the Senate was that of former national security adviser Anthony Lake, picked as director of the Central Intelligence Agency.
Lake has been criticised for his role in the United States turning a blind eye to Iranian arms flow to Bosnian Moslems.
On Feb. 11 the Senate Intelligence Committee is to start hearings on Lake that could continue over three days.
